Knackered is an informal word that means extremely tired or completely worn out. It is used in everyday speech, mainly in British, Irish, Australian, and New Zealand English. If you've ever heard British people talk, there's a good chance you've come across this word.

This is the most common meaning. When a person is knackered, they are not just a little tired — they are utterly exhausted, the kind of tiredness where your whole body feels heavy and all you want to do is sleep or sit down and do nothing.

Think of it on a scale:

A bit tired → Tired → Very tired → Exhausted → KNACKERED

It sits right at the far end of that scale. It suggests your energy is completely gone — drained, finished, used up.

Examples:

  • "I'm absolutely knackered after that long shift at work."
  • "We walked fifteen miles today. I'm completely knackered."
  • "She looked knackered — she hadn't slept properly in days."

The word can describe physical tiredness (after hard exercise, manual labour, or a long journey) as well as mental tiredness (after a stressful, draining day).

People often use the word with intensifiers like "absolutely", "completely", or "totally" to emphasise just how tired they are — but even on its own, "I'm knackered" already carries a strong sense of extreme exhaustion, so intensifiers are just extra emphasis.
Meaning 2 — Broken or Worn Out (Used for Objects and Things)

When knackered is used to describe an object, a machine, or a piece of equipment, it means that thing is broken, not working properly, or so worn out that it's no longer useful.

Examples:

  • "My old laptop is completely knackered — it won't even turn on."
  • "The washing machine is knackered. We need to buy a new one."
  • "His car's engine is knackered from years of neglect."

This meaning is very natural in casual speech. Instead of saying "broken" or "not working," a British person might simply say something is knackered.

Interestingly, knackered can also be used for body parts, and when it is, it blends both meanings above. It suggests a part of your body is damaged, worn down, or not functioning well — often from overuse or age.

Examples:

  • "My knees are knackered from years of playing football."
  • "His back is completely knackered — he's been seeing a physio for months."

Here, it doesn't just mean the body part is tired — it means it's genuinely injured or in poor condition, much like a broken machine.

Knackered is very widely used in British English — across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. It's also common in Irish English, Australian English, and New Zealand English.

It is much less familiar to speakers of American English, who would more likely say exhausted, wiped out, or beat instead.
Formality — When Can You Use It?

Knackered is an informal, colloquial word. This means it belongs in casual, everyday situations — conversations with friends, family, or colleagues you're comfortable with.

You would not use it in:

  • A formal letter or email
  • A job application
  • Academic writing
  • A professional presentation

You would use it in:

  • Chatting with a friend: "I can't come out tonight, I'm absolutely knackered."
  • Talking to a colleague casually: "That meeting went on forever — I'm knackered."
  • Describing something broken to someone you know: "Don't bother using that printer, it's knackered."

To help anchor the word in your mind, here are words with similar meanings:

For the "extremely tired" sense: exhausted, shattered, wiped out, drained, spent, worn out, dead on one's feet.

For the "broken/not working" sense: broken, bust, worn out, done for, kaput.

Knackered is simply the British informal way of expressing either of these ideas, and it does so with a great deal of colour and expressiveness — which is why it's so widely loved and used.

Use caseWhat it means
  • Person is knackered → They are utterly exhausted, with no energy left.
  • Object is knackered → It is broken or worn out and not working properly.
  • Body part is knackered → It is damaged or in poor condition, often from overuse.

It is always informal, primarily British/Irish/Australian, and sits at the extreme end of tiredness or damage — never mild.
